questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ If ${b}_{1}=5{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ from $B$ to $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =3{b}_{3}-{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4{b}_{2}-5{b}_{1}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2{b}_{1}+3{b}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & c\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $C$ relative to the basis $B$ are

$$
[{c}_{1}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{2}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{3}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].

$$

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].$
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}17 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{17}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{17} & -\frac{4}{17} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=17{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-\frac{4}{17}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 17\end{aligned}].
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/07a8e394234737d51a0064816b255569d20e826eb3a82884a24f1fc0a9fa6baa.png)
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} & -3 \\ \frac{3}{2} & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 22 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have

$$

$$
